drapeaux.note: The source is the French text of the 1898 law on Légifrance; no official English translation found, so the statement is translated from the French.

titre: The Worker No Longer Has to Prove the Boss Was at Fault
accroche: A French law of 1898 abandons a century-old rule: to be compensated, you no longer have to show that someone acted wrongly.
contenu_vulgarise:
A French worker in the nineteenth century loses a hand in a machine. To obtain compensation, the civil code requires him to show a fault by his employer. He must therefore establish that the boss acted wrongly and produce witnesses. Those witnesses are his colleagues, who risk their jobs by speaking. He must advance the costs of a trial. And if the accident comes from a badly designed machine, from anonymous negligence, or from fate, there is no fault to show, so nothing to claim.

The result is massive: the vast majority of workplace accidents give right to nothing. The maimed worker and his family fall back on charity.

## Shifting the Question

After years of parliamentary debate, the French law of April 9, 1898 changes ground. It no longer asks who was at fault, but where the risk comes from. An industry that uses machines inevitably produces accidents, not through malice but by nature. This risk is part of the activity and of its cost, just like raw materials. It must therefore be borne by the person who organizes it and profits from it.

This is called occupational risk, and it is liability without fault. The worker no longer has to prove that someone acted wrongly, only that the accident occurred in the course of work.

The compromise has a price, and it is explicit. Compensation becomes flat-rate, that is, calculated in advance according to a schedule, and partial. A permanent disability yields only a fraction of the previous wage, and the widow and orphans an even smaller share. The worker gives up full compensation for the harm suffered, which is the principle of civil law, in exchange for a certain payment.

## What This Bargain Made Possible

This trade seems unfavorable, and it is if you look at a single case. It changes everything at the scale of society, for a mechanical reason: a foreseeable, quantified risk becomes insurable. As long as compensation depended on an uncertain trial, no calculation was possible. Once the average cost of an accident is known and capped, it can be pooled among employers and provisioned in advance.

That is why the 1898 law is regularly presented as a founding text of French social protection. It was repealed by an ordinance of October 1945, and the law of October 30, 1946 brought workplace accidents into social security.

The shift is worth more than its subject. The law of liability was built on a moral idea: you pay because you acted wrongly. The 1898 law introduces an economic idea: you pay because you created the risk. The two logics have coexisted since, and the second has never stopped gaining ground, from traffic accidents to defective products.

repere.texte: The 1898 flat-rate compensation was partial: a permanent disability of 70% entitled the worker to only 55% of the previous wage, and the widow and orphans to 30% of the deceased's wage.
repere.source: Law of April 9, 1898 concerning liability for accidents suffered by workers in the course of their work, France

carte.punch: We no longer pay because someone acted wrongly, but because someone created the risk.
carte.idee: Before 1898, an injured French worker had to prove his employer's fault, with his colleagues as witnesses. The law of April 9, 1898 grants him compensation without fault, but flat-rate and partial. This now-quantifiable risk is what made insurance possible.

quiz.question: What does the French worker give up, in 1898, in exchange for compensation without fault?
choix: The possibility of bringing criminal proceedings against his employer after a serious accident
The right to full compensation for his harm, replaced by a partial flat rate calculated according to a schedule
Recourse to a judge, disputes now being settled by the labor inspectorate
Coverage of accidents occurring on the way between his home and the factory
quiz.explication: The law grants a certain payment, with no need to prove the employer's fault, but flat-rate and lower than the real harm. It is this quantifiable, capped character that made the risk insurable and poolable among employers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before 1898, why did most workplace accidents give right to no compensation, according to the entry?
choix: Because the law explicitly forbade any compensation for accidents occurring in factories
Because a fault by the boss had to be proven, which was impossible when the accident had no identifiable cause
Because the courts systematically refused to hear complaints filed by workers
Because employers were exempted from all liability by a text dating from 1804
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The civil code required proof of a fault by the employer. If the accident came from a badly designed machine or anonymous negligence, there was no fault to show, so nothing to claim.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did an occupational risk that had become quantifiable change things at the scale of society?
choix: Because the state directly took over payment of all the compensation owed
Because workers began to unionize massively from that date
Because a quantified, capped risk becomes insurable, and can be pooled among employers
Because employers stopped using machines judged too dangerous
quiz_supplementaire.explication: As long as compensation depended on an uncertain trial, no calculation was possible. A risk that has become quantifiable and capped can be pooled among employers and provisioned in advance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What became of the 1898 law, according to the entry?
choix: It remained unchanged and still applies as is today
It was invalidated by a court decision as early as 1910 for unconstitutionality
It was extended in 1920 to also cover household accidents
It was repealed in 1945, with workplace accidents joining social security in 1946
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1898 law was repealed by an ordinance of October 1945, and the law of October 30, 1946 brought workplace accidents into social security.
